title: UPSC Mains
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public UPSC Civil Services Mains syllabus. Not a capture of past questions.

items.stem: A civil servant is asked to approve a file that benefits a company in which a close relative holds a large stake. Which course of action best reflects the principle of avoiding conflict of interest?
options: Recuse from the decision and disclose the relationship to the competent authority
Approve the file quickly since the merits are unrelated to the relative
Approve the file but keep the relationship confidential
Ask the relative to sell the stake only after approval is granted
items.explanation: Conflict of interest is managed by disclosure and recusal so that an untainted authority decides; secrecy, hurried approval, or post-hoc divestment do not remove the conflict.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: A district officer learns that a government scheme meant for tribal welfare bypasses the most remote hamlets. Empathy in public administration would most appropriately lead the officer to
options: sit in the office and wait for written complaints
personally visit the hamlets to understand the barriers and redesign delivery
blame the field staff for poor implementation and transfer them
report the scheme as successful because the funds were spent
items.explanation: Empathy requires understanding the lived situation of beneficiaries and acting on it; waiting, blaming, or window-dressing does not address the exclusion.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Probity in governance is best described as
options: obedience to the orders of political superiors
the quality of holding strong personal opinions
adherence to the highest standards of honesty and incorruptibility in public dealings
maximising the budget of one's own department
items.explanation: Probity is uncompromising integrity and uprightness in the use of public office; it is not mere obedience, opinionatedness, or empire-building.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: A junior officer receives an order that is legal but ethically dubious. According to the idea of conscientious objection, the officer should
options: obey without question because orders must always be followed
leak the order to the media immediately
resign silently without informing anyone
record reasoned concerns through proper channels before complying
items.explanation: Conscientious objection in administration means documenting dissent through legitimate channels while respecting hierarchy; blind obedience, leaks, and silent exit avoid responsibility.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Whistleblowing in a public organisation is ethically justified primarily when
options: the disclosure reveals serious wrongdoing and internal remedies have been exhausted
an employee wants revenge against a supervisor
the employee is about to resign for personal reasons
the information is already public gossip
items.explanation: Whistleblowing is justified by a serious public-interest wrong and by first exhausting internal corrective avenues; revenge, resignation, or gossip lack this ethical basis.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Moral courage in the civil services is demonstrated when an officer
options: takes the popular stand to win public applause
stands by an ethical decision despite pressure from powerful interests
avoids any decision that may attract criticism
follows the majority opinion in every meeting
items.explanation: Moral courage is the willingness to act rightly under pressure and at personal cost; crowd-pleasing, risk-aversion, and majoritarianism are its opposites.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Tolerance as a civic virtue in a plural society requires
options: suppressing opinions that differ from the majority
treating all opinions as equally factually valid
respecting and engaging with viewpoints one disagrees with
avoiding all public discussion of differences
items.explanation: Tolerance means respecting the right of others to hold different views and engaging them, not suppressing dissent, collapsing truth into opinion, or silencing debate.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: A compassionate administrator dealing with a destitute elderly applicant would
options: demand documents the applicant cannot produce before giving any help
send the applicant away because the matter is not a priority
give personal money and close the file
recognise the applicant's vulnerability and facilitate access within the rules
items.explanation: Compassion in administration means recognising vulnerability and enabling lawful assistance; rigid demand, indifference, or private charity do not serve the public duty.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: The principle of integrity in public life differs from mere loyalty because integrity
options: demands consistency with ethical principles even against one's own group
requires unquestioning support for one's organisation
means never disagreeing with superiors
is the same as personal popularity
items.explanation: Integrity is fidelity to ethical principles, which may require resisting one's own organisation; loyalty to a group or superior is a narrower, sometimes conflicting, value.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: A policy maximises total welfare but gravely harms a small minority. A deontological critic would object mainly because
options: total welfare is impossible to calculate
the minority's rights are being violated regardless of aggregate benefit
the policy is not popular with the majority
the policy costs too much to implement
items.explanation: Deontology judges actions by duties and rights, so harming some as a means to aggregate welfare violates their rights; cost, popularity, and measurability are different objections.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Accountability in public service is strengthened most when
options: officials are never questioned by superiors
files are kept confidential to protect officials
decisions are documented and subject to review and answerability
responsibility is diffused among many departments
items.explanation: Accountability requires records, review, and the duty to answer for decisions; secrecy and diffused responsibility dilute rather than strengthen it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: The relationship between attitude and aptitude in administration is best captured by the idea that
options: aptitude alone guarantees ethical conduct
attitude is irrelevant once skills are high
attitude and aptitude cannot coexist
a sound attitude channels aptitude toward the public good
items.explanation: Aptitude supplies capability while attitude supplies direction; high skill without a public-spirited attitude can be misused, so the two are complementary, not substitutes.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Emotional intelligence helps a civil servant most directly by
options: recognising and regulating emotions to make balanced decisions
eliminating all emotional reactions
allowing anger to drive quick enforcement
avoiding any contact with aggrieved citizens
items.explanation: Emotional intelligence is awareness and regulation of one's own and others' emotions for sound decisions; suppression, anger-driven action, and avoidance are contrary to it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Gandhi's insistence that means must be as pure as ends implies that
options: any method is acceptable if the goal is noble
unjust means corrupt even a worthy goal
ends are irrelevant so long as means are pure
social change requires secrecy and force
items.explanation: Gandhi held that means and ends are inseparable, so violent or dishonest means taint the outcome; the others either justify any means or ignore ends, which he rejected.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: The ethic of nishkam karma, action without attachment to results, chiefly directs a public servant to
options: avoid responsibility for outcomes altogether
work only when recognition is assured
perform duty sincerely without craving personal reward
abandon action during difficult times
items.explanation: Nishkam karma is detached, sincere performance of duty; it does not mean irresponsibility, reward-seeking, or inaction, which the doctrine explicitly rejects.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: A government officer is offered an expensive gift by a contractor whose tender is pending. The most ethical response is to
options: accept it as a customary courtesy
accept it but reciprocate later
accept it and award the tender on merit alone
politely decline and record the offer
items.explanation: Declining a gift from an interested party and documenting it protects impartiality; acceptance, even with reciprocation or a fair award, creates obligation and suspicion.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: An officer faces strong family pressure to favour a relative in a recruitment matter. The officer should
options: decline, disclosing the conflict and letting an unrelated authority decide
comply, since family duty outweighs public duty
comply secretly to preserve family harmony
delay the matter indefinitely to avoid the issue
items.explanation: Public duty overrides private gain; disclosure and delegation to an untainted authority resolve the conflict openly, whereas compliance, secrecy, or indefinite delay are evasions.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Transparency in administration and legitimate secrecy are best balanced by
options: disclosing everything without exception
disclosing all that is not justifiably exempt in the public interest
keeping everything secret for efficiency
leaving the choice to the personal whim of each official
items.explanation: Transparency is the norm and secrecy the narrowly justified exception for defined public interests, not absolute disclosure, blanket secrecy, or arbitrary discretion.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Restorative justice emphasises forgiveness and reparation, which may tension with retributive justice because
options: restorative justice ignores victims entirely
retributive justice never punishes offenders
restorative justice prioritises healing while retribution prioritises deserved punishment
the two are identical in every respect
items.explanation: The two approaches have different aims, repairing harm versus proportionate punishment; restorative justice does not ignore victims, and neither ignores offender responsibility.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Large development projects displace communities. From an ethical standpoint, the strongest justification for such projects requires that
options: the projects maximise national GDP regardless of local harm
protesters are removed to speed up construction
compensation is paid only after resettlement is complete
displaced people are compensated, rehabilitated, and genuinely consent
items.explanation: Ethical development demands informed consent plus fair compensation and rehabilitation; pure GDP maximisation, suppression of dissent, or delayed compensation fail on justice grounds.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Essay and Ethics

items.stem: Indian federalism is often described as quasi-federal mainly because
options: the Constitution combines a strong centre with federal features such as a division of powers
states have no constitutionally guaranteed powers
the centre cannot legislate on state subjects
states may secede from the Union at will
items.explanation: India has a federal division of powers plus a strong centre with unitary features, hence quasi-federal; states do have guaranteed powers and cannot secede, and the centre can legislate in defined matters.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Judicial review in India empowers the judiciary to
options: amend the Constitution at will
declare laws inconsistent with the Constitution void
overrule Parliament on purely political questions
appoint the Chief Election Commissioner
items.explanation: Judicial review tests legislation against the Constitution and voids inconsistency; courts neither amend the Constitution nor decide political questions or make executive appointments.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: When a Fundamental Right and a Directive Principle appear to conflict, courts generally
options: treat Directive Principles as superior to Fundamental Rights
ignore Fundamental Rights completely
harmonise them, giving effect to both as far as possible
strike down the Directive Principle as void
items.explanation: The Supreme Court seeks harmonious construction, reading rights and directive principles together; directive principles are not superior, and neither set is simply ignored or void.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: An active civil society strengthens democracy chiefly by
options: replacing elected legislatures in law-making
contesting elections as a parallel government
enforcing laws in place of the police
articulating citizens' concerns and holding power accountable
items.explanation: Civil society mobilises voice and accountability; it does not legislate, function as an alternative government, or perform police enforcement, which are state functions.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment is significant because it
options: gave constitutional status to rural local self-government with regular elections
abolished panchayats in urban areas
centralised all rural funds in the Union government
removed reservations for women
items.explanation: The amendment constitutionally entrenched panchayats, mandated regular elections, and provided reservations including for women; it did not abolish urban bodies, centralise funds, or remove reservations.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The Right to Information strengthens accountability mainly by
options: allowing citizens to amend official records
enabling citizens to access official information and question decisions
prosecuting officials automatically for every error
replacing the need for an independent judiciary
items.explanation: RTI empowers citizens with information to scrutinise decisions; it neither lets them alter records nor auto-prosecutes officials, and it complements rather than replaces the judiciary.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The doctrine of separation of powers is reflected in the Indian Constitution, but with
options: a complete absence of checks and balances
the executive controlling the judiciary completely
a system of checks and balances among the three organs
the judiciary making all executive appointments
items.explanation: Indian constitutionalism blends separation with checks and balances; no organ fully controls another, and there is neither an absence of checks nor judicial control over all appointments.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: State funding of elections is often proposed as an electoral reform primarily to
options: ban all political parties
eliminate the need for elections
give the ruling party an unfair advantage
reduce the influence of unaccounted money in politics
items.explanation: Public funding aims to curb the corrupting role of undisclosed money; it does not ban parties, replace elections, or favour the incumbent, which would defeat its purpose.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The Governor's discretionary powers in state administration are constitutionally intended to
options: be exercised in limited, defined situations such as recommending President's Rule
allow the Governor to govern the state directly
override the elected Council of Ministers routinely
replace the role of the Chief Minister permanently
items.explanation: Discretion is confined to defined contingencies and is not a licence to govern or permanently displace the elected ministry, whose advice the Governor normally follows.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The anti-defection law principally seeks to
options: encourage frequent floor-crossing for personal gain
curb defection by disqualifying legislators who abandon their party
abolish the office of the Speaker
prevent legislators from voting at all
items.explanation: The law deters defection by disqualifying members for specified conduct; it does not encourage crossing, abolish the Speaker's office, or bar voting.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The bureaucracy contributes to sound policy mainly by
options: framing policy solely to please political masters
ignoring legal procedures in the interest of speed
providing evidence-based advice and implementing policy impartially
contesting elections on a party platform
items.explanation: A professional civil service offers objective advice and impartial implementation; sycophancy, procedural shortcuts, and electoral activity violate its neutral role.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: E-governance improves service delivery, but its chief equity risk is
options: too much transparency for officials
citizens learning to use technology
reduced paperwork in government offices
a digital divide that excludes the poor and the digitally illiterate
items.explanation: Digital delivery can bypass those without devices, connectivity, or literacy unless alternate channels are kept; the other options describe benefits or minor issues, not equity risk.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Criminalisation of politics is best addressed by
options: fast-tracking trials of cases against candidates and disclosing criminal antecedents
barring all candidates with any pending case permanently
abolishing political parties altogether
letting voters ignore candidates' records
items.explanation: Reform centres on speedy trials and public disclosure so voters can decide on facts; blanket permanent disqualification, abolishing parties, or concealing records are disproportionate or evasive.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Departmental Standing Committees of Parliament strengthen legislative scrutiny by
options: taking over the Prime Minister's executive powers
examining demands for grants and scrutinising legislation in detail
conducting court trials of ministers
framing the annual budget without any oversight
items.explanation: Committees provide detailed, informed scrutiny of finances and bills; they do not exercise executive power, try cases, or shield the budget from oversight.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Cooperative federalism is best illustrated by
options: the Union unilaterally withdrawing a state's powers
states refusing to implement central laws
institutions such as the GST Council where centre and states decide jointly
the abolition of all state legislatures
items.explanation: Cooperative federalism institutionalises joint decision-making, as in the GST Council; unilateral withdrawal, non-implementation, and abolition of legislatures are its opposites.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Judicial activism becomes a concern when courts
options: enforce Fundamental Rights against the state
interpret statutes to protect citizens
hear public interest litigation at all
assume the functions of the legislature or executive through sweeping directions
items.explanation: The criticism is about overreach into policy domains reserved to elected organs; enforcing rights and interpreting statutes are legitimate judicial functions, and PIL itself is not the objection.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Political neutrality of the civil service requires that officials
options: serve the government of the day impartially without partisan allegiance
publicly campaign for a party after office hours
refuse to implement lawful government policy
leak policy differences to the press
items.explanation: Neutrality means loyal, impartial service to the lawful government irrespective of party; campaigning, obstruction, and leaks violate the service's political neutrality.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Decentralised local government improves accountability because it
options: moves decisions further away from citizens
brings decision-making closer to those affected by it
removes the need for state legislatures
concentrates all power in district collectors
items.explanation: Subsidiarity places decisions near citizens, improving responsiveness; decentralisation does not distance decisions, abolish higher tiers, or centralise power in one officer.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: Constitutional morality in public life implies fidelity to
options: the personal morality of the ruling party
majority sentiment at all times
core constitutional values and processes, even when inconvenient
the preferences of senior officials
items.explanation: Constitutional morality binds actors to constitutional values and procedures over majoritarian convenience; it is not party doctrine, passing majority will, or official privilege.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: The rule of law in a constitutional democracy requires that
options: the executive be above the law
laws apply only to citizens and not to the state
official discretion be entirely unlimited
no person, including officials, is above the law and all are subject to it
items.explanation: The rule of law means equality before and accountability under law for everyone, including the state; executive supremacy, state immunity, and unlimited discretion negate it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Governance and Polity

items.stem: To control demand-pull inflation, a central bank would most likely
options: raise the policy interest rate to dampen demand
lower the repo rate to encourage borrowing
print more currency to increase money supply
reduce the cash reserve ratio to boost lending
items.explanation: Demand-pull inflation is cooled by tightening monetary policy such as raising rates; cutting rates, printing money, or lowering reserve requirements would stimulate demand and worsen inflation.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A persistently high fiscal deficit is concerning chiefly because it
options: always guarantees higher economic growth
may crowd out private investment and create debt-servicing burdens
has no effect on the economy
eliminates the need for taxation
items.explanation: Large persistent deficits can raise borrowing costs, crowd out private investment, and burden future budgets; deficits are not automatically growth-enhancing, neutral, or a substitute for revenue.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: The Goods and Services Tax is described as a destination-based tax because it is levied
options: at the point of origin of goods
only on exports
where consumption finally takes place
only on agricultural produce
items.explanation: Under GST, revenue accrues to the consuming state, hence destination-based; origin-based levying, export-only, or agriculture-only application misdescribe it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A key structural constraint on MSME credit in India is
options: excessive reliance on audited financial statements by lenders
MSMEs refusing all forms of institutional credit
an oversupply of formal-sector jobs for MSME owners
insufficient collateral and information that make lenders reluctant to lend
items.explanation: MSMEs often lack collateral and documented financials, raising perceived risk and creating credit gaps; lenders typically face a dearth, not a surfeit, of reliable financials, and the other options are unrelated.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Agricultural input subsidies are criticised primarily because they
options: distort cropping patterns and strain fiscal resources
never reach any farmer
reduce farm output to zero
benefit only large export houses
items.explanation: Subsidies can skew cropping choices and burden public finances; they do reach farmers, do not eliminate output, and their equity impact is debated but not limited to exporters.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: India's climate commitments under the Paris Agreement are chiefly delivered through
options: binding emission cuts enforced by foreign courts
Nationally Determined Contributions covering mitigation and adaptation
withdrawal from all climate treaties
unilateral trade sanctions on neighbouring countries
items.explanation: The Paris framework is built on self-determined, nationally communicated contributions; it does not impose foreign judicial enforcement, treaty exit, or trade sanctions as its delivery route.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: The shift to renewable energy creates a grid challenge mainly because solar and wind power are
options: always more expensive than coal
impossible to transmit over long distances
intermittent, requiring storage and grid balancing
unavailable across most of India
items.explanation: The variability of solar and wind needs storage, backup, and balancing; they are increasingly cost-competitive, transmittable, and widely available, so the other options are inaccurate.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A circular economy most directly aims to
options: maximise the extraction of virgin materials
ban all manufacturing activity
increase the volume of landfill waste
keep resources in use through reuse, repair, and recycling
items.explanation: Circularity reduces waste by retaining value through reuse and recycling; it is the antithesis of extraction-maximising and landfill-increasing linear models, and it does not ban manufacturing.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Biodiversity conservation is economically justified because ecosystems
options: provide services such as pollination, water regulation, and climate stability
have no measurable value to society
can always be replaced cheaply by technology
exist only to generate tourism revenue
items.explanation: Ecosystem services underpin agriculture, water, and climate stability, giving conservation a strong economic rationale; denying value, assuming cheap substitutes, or reducing nature to tourism misjudges it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A robust Environmental Impact Assessment serves to
options: approve projects automatically to save time
identify and mitigate environmental harm before approval
replace all environmental laws
guarantee that no project harms the environment
items.explanation: EIA anticipates impacts and prescribes mitigation as a condition of clearance; it is not a rubber stamp, does not supersede laws, and cannot guarantee zero harm.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Rapid urbanisation in India strains infrastructure chiefly because
options: cities have a large surplus of housing
rural areas have no population
population growth outpaces planned water, transport, and waste systems
urban planning is unnecessary
items.explanation: Urban systems lag behind population influx, causing service deficits; there is no housing surplus in this context, rural areas remain populated, and planning is essential, not redundant.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Measuring poverty solely by income tends to understate deprivation because it ignores
options: how much money a household earns
the market value of a household's assets
whether a household owns a television
access to health, education, and basic services
items.explanation: Multidimensional poverty looks beyond income to health, education, and living standards; ignoring these understates deprivation, whereas earnings and assets are already captured and the television example is trivial.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A large informal sector weakens worker welfare mainly because informal workers
options: lack social security, contracts, and effective legal protection
enjoy guaranteed social security
are always higher paid than formal workers
do not need any income
items.explanation: Informality is marked by absent social security, job security, and legal cover; informal workers are not guaranteed benefits, are typically lower paid, and obviously need income.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Financial inclusion contributes to inclusive growth by
options: restricting banking services to large cities
extending formal financial services such as accounts and credit to the excluded
discouraging savings among the poor
replacing all cash transactions with barter
items.explanation: Inclusion brings the unbanked into formal savings, credit, and insurance, supporting growth; restricting access, discouraging saving, or reverting to barter would do the opposite.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling communities primarily to
options: evict them from forests
transfer all forests to mining companies
secure their individual and community rights over forest land and resources
ban all tribal habitation in forests
items.explanation: The Act vests recognised rights and resource use in forest communities; eviction, corporate transfer, and habitation bans contradict its purpose.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Groundwater depletion in India is aggravated most by
options: strict regulation of tube wells
reduced use of irrigation
excessive rainwater harvesting
free or subsidised power that encourages excessive pumping
items.explanation: Subsidised electricity lowers pumping costs and spurs over-extraction; regulation and rainwater harvesting mitigate depletion, while reduced irrigation does not aggravate it.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: A carbon tax on emissions is primarily intended to
options: internalise the environmental cost of emissions into prices
make polluting activities cheaper
subsidise fossil fuel use
ban all industrial production
items.explanation: A carbon price makes emitters bear the social cost, steering behaviour; cheapening pollution, subsidising fossil fuels, or banning industry would defeat that intent.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: Green hydrogen is attractive as a clean fuel because it
options: is produced from coal without any emissions
can be made from water using renewable electricity with no direct carbon emissions
is chemically identical to natural gas
can be used only in petrol engines
items.explanation: Green hydrogen uses renewable-powered electrolysis of water; coal-based production is brown or grey, it differs from natural gas, and it is used in industry and fuel cells, not as petrol.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: From an economic perspective, investing in disaster preparedness is justified because
options: disasters never recur
relief is always cheaper than prevention
ex-ante mitigation reduces future losses far more than repeated relief spending
insurance can eliminate all disaster risk
items.explanation: Prevention and mitigation cut expected losses cost-effectively compared with repeated relief; disasters do recur, relief is not always cheaper, and insurance transfers rather than removes risk.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment

items.stem: The core tension between economic growth and environmental sustainability arises because
options: growth and environment can never be reconciled in any policy
sustainability requires zero economic activity
environmental protection always destroys the economy
conventional growth can deplete natural capital unless decoupled from resource use
items.explanation: The challenge is decoupling growth from resource depletion and pollution; reconciliation is possible, sustainability does not mean zero activity, and protection need not destroy the economy.
items.reference: UPSC Mains Syllabus - Economy and Environment
